title: Efficacy of a Rhythm-based Serious Game for Improving Executive Functions in Individuals with Neurocognitive Deficits: a Randomized Controlled Trial
summary:
Research in recent years has shown that musical and rhythmic training can help improve people's cognitive performance. This type of training is of particular interest when it comes to difficulties with attention and executive functions. Executive functions are a group of mental skills that enable us to plan, organise, control and carry out complex tasks. They are the 'control system' of our brain and play an important role in regulating our behaviour, problem solving, self-control and adapting to new situations. However, more research is needed to show whether rhythm training can improve these abilities and be used as a therapy. 
The aim of this study is to find out whether digital rhythmic training program is useful in the neuropsychological rehabilitation of people with acquired brain injury. To do so, participants will train with the "Rhythm Workers" app on a tablet over a period of 4 weeks. Before and after this training period, we will perform a series of neuropsychological and rhythmic tasks to find out if their skills have improved as a result of the training. After three months there will be another test to assess the long-term effects. We also want to find out if the training works better for some people than others.
conditions: Individuals with an acquired brain injury and a structural deficit (confirmed by MRI or CT) and cognitive deficits in executive functions or attention (objectifiable or subjectively reported)

interventions.name: Intervention group (IG): independent home training using the "Rhythm Workers" app (Bégel et al., 2018) for 4 weeks. Participants are required to train five times a week for 20-30 minutes each. There will be short weekly telephone contacts with the study team.
Waitlist control group (WCG) starting training after 4 weeks.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
(1) acquired brain injury with a structural deficit (confirmed by MRI or CT), (2) an elapsed time since injury of at least three month, (3) cognitive deficits in executive functions or attention (objectifiable or subjectively reported), (4) willingness and ability to participate, and (5) complete informed consent form.
Exclusion criteria:
(1) motor, hearing, or comprehension deficits that do not allow participation, (2) severe psychiatric disorder, (3) alcohol / drug abuse, (4) evidence for media addiction, (5) professional musicians, (6) pregnancy or planned pregnancy, breastfeeding women, (7) intensive neuropsychological therapy over the last three months (i.e. inpatient or day-clinic). Continuation of outpatient treatment will be registered.
